steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on standardizing the evaluation of conditional image generation models. Describe the inconsistency problem in current evaluations, the components of our framework (dataset, inference library, human evaluation), and the main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Rise of conditional image generation and its many tasks
- Problem: inconsistent experimental setups (dataset, inference, evaluation)
- Need for a centralized, continuous evaluation effort: ImagenHub
- ImagenHub Dataset
- ImagenHub Inference Library
- ImagenHub Evaluator
- Main observations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - diffusion models -> image generation one of the most popular AI research areas
  - many conditional image generation models in the past year for controllability
  - text-guided image generation (ground on a text prompt); subject-conditioned generation, text-guided editing, multi-subject-conditioned generation, style-guided generation
  - subject-level, background-level, style-level controls for downstream applications
  - fast pace, many reported improvements, but inconsistent experimental setups
- Three inconsistencies
  - dataset: each work curates its own evaluation set -> incomparable
  - inference: heavy hyper-parameter tuning and prompt engineering -> less robust; unequal tuning effort -> unfair comparison
  - evaluation: different human evaluation protocols/guidelines; single rater or no inter-worker agreement -> results not comparable across papers
- Need
  - impossible to track real progress; hinders the field
  - centralized, continuous effort to fairly evaluate every model
  - goal: standardize serving and evaluation of all open-source conditional image generation models; modules in Figure 1
- ImagenHub Dataset
  - surveyed public evaluation sets, picked diverse instances
  - 7 subsets, 100-200 instances each; standardized input
- ImagenHub Inference Library
  - ported dispersed codebases into a unified format
  - fixed hyper-parameters and prompt format, no per-instance tuning -> fair, reproducible
  - easily extendable; Appendix A.7, A.8, A.9
- ImagenHub Evaluator
  - explored metrics, iterated rating guidelines for inter-rater agreement
  - two three-valued metrics: 'Semantic Consistency', 'Perceptual Quality'; Fleiss Kappa, Krippendorff's Alpha
  - benefits: unambiguous checklist table; unified across tasks; sustainability (individual rating, reuse of results)
- Observations (Figure 2: best and medium model; section 5)
  - performance generally unsatisfying except Text-guided Image Generation and Subject-driven Image Generation
  - published results mostly consistent: 83% of rankings match ours
  - automatic metrics correlate poorly with human preference except subject-driven generation; correlation below 0.2

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Image generation has quickly become one of the most popular research areas in AI, with the recent development of diffusion models. In the past year a lot of conditional image generation models were proposed to make the image generation process controllable. Many different conditions have been tried for steering the diffusion process. Text-guided image generation is one of the most popular tasks, and it aims to generate the corresponding image grounded on a text prompt. There are also other tasks like subject-conditioned image generation, text-guided image editing, multi-subject-conditioned image generation, style-guided image generation, etc. These tasks serve different kinds of downstream applications by enabling subject-level, background-level and style-level controls. The field moves at an unprecedented pace and published papers report lots of improvements. But one big issue we see is that the published works are very inconsistent in their experimental setups. The inconsistencies come mainly from three aspects, dataset, inference and evaluation:

- Dataset: Existing works curate their own evaluation dataset, so the different models are totally incomparable.

- Inference: Some works need heavy hyper-parameter tuning and prompt engineering to get reasonable performance, so the model is less robust. Since the tuning effort is very different between models, comparing them could become unfair.

- Evaluation: Existing works use different human evaluation protocols and guidelines. Because of this it is impossible to compare human evaluation scores across methods. Also, some works use only one rater or do not report inter-worker agreement. So the reported results might not be comparable across papers.

Because of these three inconsistencies it is nearly impossible to track the real progress in conditional image generation, and this could greatly hinder the development of the field. What is needed is a centralized effort to evaluate every model fairly. This effort also has to be continuous so it keeps up with how the field evolves. Our paper aims to do this, to standardize the serving and evaluation of all open-source conditional image generation models. ImagenHub consists of the modules in Figure 1.

ImagenHub modules (Figure 1):
- Dataset
  - surveyed public evaluation sets, diverse instances
  - 7 subsets, 100-200 instances each; standardized input
- Inference Library
  - port dispersed codebases, unified format
  - fixed hyper-parameters and prompt format -> fair, reproducible
  - extendable; Appendix A.7, A.8, A.9
- Evaluator
  - iterate on rating guidelines for inter-rater agreement
  - 'Semantic Consistency' and 'Perceptual Quality' (three-valued); Fleiss Kappa, Krippendorff's Alpha
  - checklist table; unified across tasks; sustainability
- Observations (Figure 2, section 5)
  - unsatisfying except text-guided and subject-driven generation
  - 83% of published rankings consistent with ours
  - automatic metrics vs human preference: correlation lower than 0.2 (except subject-driven)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Image generation has quickly become one of the most popular research areas in AI, with the recent development of diffusion models. In the past year a lot of conditional image generation models were proposed to make the image generation process controllable. Many different conditions have been tried for steering the diffusion process. Text-guided image generation is one of the most popular tasks, and it aims to generate the corresponding image grounded on a text prompt. There are also other tasks like subject-conditioned image generation, text-guided image editing, multi-subject-conditioned image generation, style-guided image generation, etc. These tasks serve different kinds of downstream applications by enabling subject-level, background-level and style-level controls. The field moves at an unprecedented pace and published papers report lots of improvements. But one big issue we see is that the published works are very inconsistent in their experimental setups. The inconsistencies come mainly from three aspects, dataset, inference and evaluation:

- Dataset: Existing works curate their own evaluation dataset, so the different models are totally incomparable.

- Inference: Some works need heavy hyper-parameter tuning and prompt engineering to get reasonable performance, so the model is less robust. Since the tuning effort is very different between models, comparing them could become unfair.

- Evaluation: Existing works use different human evaluation protocols and guidelines. Because of this it is impossible to compare human evaluation scores across methods. Also, some works use only one rater or do not report inter-worker agreement. So the reported results might not be comparable across papers.

Because of these three inconsistencies it is nearly impossible to track the real progress in conditional image generation, and this could greatly hinder the development of the field. What is needed is a centralized effort to evaluate every model fairly. This effort also has to be continuous so it keeps up with how the field evolves. Our paper aims to do this, to standardize the serving and evaluation of all open-source conditional image generation models. ImagenHub consists of the modules in Figure 1.

ImagenHub Dataset. We surveyed the existing public evaluation sets for all the generation tasks and picked diverse instances from them to build the ImagenHub dataset. It has 7 subsets, and each has 100-200 instances. The dataset is meant to standardize the evaluation input so that the comparison of different models is fair.

ImagenHub Inference Library. We built an ImagenHub library for evaluating all the conditional image generation models. We ported the very dispersed codebases of existing works and standardized them into one unified format. For inference, we fixed the hyper-parameters and the prompt format so there is no per-instance prompt or hyper-parameter tuning, and this makes inference of the different models fair and reproducible. The library is designed to be easy to extend. Appendix A.7, A.8, and A.9 show how third parties and researchers can benefit from our work.

ImagenHub Evaluator. We tried different human evaluation metrics and went through different versions of the rating guidelines to improve inter-rater agreement. In the end we used two three-valued rating metrics, ‘Semantic Consistency’ and ‘Perceptual Quality’, which get generally high inter-worker agreement measured by Fleiss Kappa and Krippendorff’s Alpha. The rating standard we designed has several benefits: (1) the rating guide is an unambiguous checklist table so raters can rate the image easily. (2) The rating guideline is the same for every task type. (3) Sustainability. Each model is rated individually, so previous evaluation results can be reused when new models are added.

Figure 2 shows our evaluation results, with the overall score of the best-performing model and the medium-performing model. From the evaluation results in section 5 we made some general observations:

- The performance of existing models is generally unsatisfying, except for Text-guided Image Generation and Subject-driven Image Generation.

- Evaluation results from the published papers are generally consistent with our evaluation. 83% of the published result ranking is consistent with our ranking.

- Automatic evaluation metrics do not correlate well with human preference except for subject-driven image generation. The correlation scores are lower than 0.2.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
With the recent development of diffusion models, image generation has quickly become one of the most popular research areas in AI. To enable controllability in the image generation process, a myriad of conditional image generation models have been proposed in the past year, and a diverse set of conditions has been attempted to steer the diffusion process. One of the most popular tasks is text-guided image generation [1,2,3], which aims to ground on a text prompt to generate the corresponding image. Besides that, there are also subject-conditioned image generation [4,5], text-guided image editing [6], multi-subject-conditioned image generation [7], style-guided image generation [8], etc. These different tasks aim to serve different types of downstream applications by enabling subject-level, background-level and style-level controls. The field is evolving at an unprecedented pace and lots of improvements have been reported in published papers. However, one glaring issue we observed is that the published works are highly inconsistent in their experimental setups. The inconsistencies mainly come from three aspects, namely dataset, inference and evaluation:

- Dataset: The existing works curated their own evaluation datasets, which makes the different models totally incomparable.

- Inference: Some works require heavy hyper-parameter tuning and prompt engineering to achieve reasonable performance, which makes the model less robust. Since the tuning effort differs significantly between models, their comparison could become unfair.

- Evaluation: The existing works used different human evaluation protocols and guidelines, which renders it impossible to compare human evaluation scores across different methods. Moreover, some of the works either employ a single rater or do not report inter-worker agreement. Thus, the reported results might not be comparable across different papers.

These three inconsistencies make it nearly impossible to track the real progress in the field of conditional image generation, which could greatly hinder its development. The desiderata is a centralized effort to fairly evaluate every model. More importantly, this effort needs to be continuous to keep up with the evolution of the field. Our paper aims to serve this purpose by standardizing the serving and evaluation of all open-source conditional image generation models. More specifically, ImagenHub consists of the modules listed in Figure 1.

ImagenHub Dataset. We surveyed the existing public evaluation sets for all the generation tasks and picked diverse instances from them to build our ImagenHub dataset, which consists of 7 subsets, each with 100-200 instances. This dataset aims at standardizing the evaluation input to ensure fair comparison of different models.

ImagenHub Inference Library. We built an ImagenHub library to evaluate all the conditional image generation models. We ported the highly dispersed codebases of the existing works and standardized them into a unified format. During inference, we fixed the hyper-parameters and the prompt format to prevent per-instance prompt or hyper-parameter tuning, which makes the inference of different models fair and reproducible. The library is designed to be easily extendable. Appendix A.7, A.8, and A.9 show how third parties and researchers can benefit from our work.

ImagenHub Evaluator. We explored different human evaluation metrics and iterated over different versions of the rating guidelines to improve the inter-rater agreement. We settled on two three-valued rating metrics, ‘Semantic Consistency’ and ‘Perceptual Quality’, which achieve generally high inter-worker agreement measured by Fleiss Kappa [11] and Krippendorff’s Alpha [12]. Our rating standard is designed to achieve several benefits: (1) The rating guide is an unambiguous checklist table so that the rater can rate the image with ease. (2) The rating guideline is unified across every task type. (3) Sustainability. Since each model is rated individually, previous evaluation results can be reused when new models are added.

We show our evaluation results in Figure 2, with the overall score of the best-performing model and the medium-performing model. Based on our evaluation results in section 5, we made some general observations:

- The existing models’ performance is generally unsatisfying except for Text-guided Image Generation and Subject-driven Image Generation.

- Evaluation results from the published papers are generally consistent with our evaluation: 83% of the published result ranking is consistent with our ranking.

- Automatic evaluation metrics do not correlate well with human preference except for subject-driven image generation, with correlation scores lower than 0.2.
